bib.title: Unlocking the Power of Multi-Agent LLM for Reasoning: From Lazy Agents to Deliberation

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Unlocking the Power of Multi-Agent LLM for Reasoning: From Lazy Agents to Deliberation" (Dr. MAMR), Zhiwei Zhang, Xiaomin Li, Yudi Lin, Hui Liu, Ramraj Chandradevan, Linlin Wu, Minhua Lin, Fali Wang, Xianfeng Tang, Qi He, Suhang Wang (Penn State, Harvard, MSU, Utah, Microsoft). arXiv 2511.02303v1, 4 Nov 2025. Header says "preprint"; no venue.

COVERAGE: 85,402 of 85,402 chars of the extraction. I read the body and all appendices (A-I) in full. The reference list (about chars 31,000-61,000) was only skimmed for origins. Extraction is clean apart from garbled equations and axis text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. A trained multi-agent pair loses to a single agent on average. Setup: Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct, trained on DeepScaleR, pass@1 on 7 math benchmarks. ReMA is the two-agent baseline, with a meta-thinking agent and a reasoning agent sharing one set of weights. On 7B the average is 55.08 for single-agent GRPO, 51.97 for ReMA and 58.43 for Dr. MAMR. On 14B it is 58.05, 57.24 and 62.49.
 quote: "ReMA consistently underperforms compared to single-agent GRPO, highlighting the severity of the lazy agent issue and its detrimental effect on multi-agent performance."
 where: Sec 6.2, p.8; Table 1 (average rows: 55.08/51.97/58.43; 58.05/57.24/62.49).
2. Lazy-agent collapse: one agent dominates. The reasoning agent's causal influence decays toward zero while the meta-thinking agent's grows. The system becomes an effective single agent. Setup: ReMA, 7B, training steps 0-80. Influence is measured by suppressing attention to a step and taking the KL divergence on the next step.
 quote: "the reasoning agent's causal influence initially increases slightly at the beginning of training but then steadily decreases, eventually approaching zero, while the meta-thinking agent's influence grows significantly as it comes to dominate the reasoning process."
 where: Sec 6.3, p.8. Related: Sec 4 shows MATH500 at 75.0 untrained and 74.4 after ReMA training.
3. Root cause is a loss bias. Multi-turn GRPO divides by the number of turns (1/T_i). Per Theorem 1, if two trajectories earn equal reward, the shorter one is favoured unless the longer one's gradient contribution is at least T_L/T_S times larger. Lazy behaviour (empty or copied outputs) gives shorter trajectories. Evidence is the mean-turns curve over the first 20 training steps (Fig 5, App F).
 quote: "the normalization bias steers optimization toward trajectories with fewer turns, and reasoning processes exhibiting lazy behavior naturally produce shorter trajectories, thereby receiving preferential reinforcement during training."
 number: none (Theorem 1 is the finding). where: Sec 5.1, p.5; proof in App E.
4. Prompting alone only partly fixes it. Setup: ReMA, 7B-scale, MATH500.
 quote: "Adding a prompt to encourage non-trivial responses narrows the causal-effect gap and improves performance from 74.4 to 75.6. However, the reasoning agent still shows weaker influence than in the baseline, and the modest 0.6-point gain suggests reliance on shortcuts"
 where: Sec 4, pp.4-5. Dr. MAMR scores 78.4 in the same Fig 2 comparison.
5. Ablation: removing each piece hurts. Setup: 7B; AIME24, AMC23, Gaokao2023en, Olympiad Bench. Full model scores 20.00 / 62.50 / 65.20 / 52.34. Without normalization debias (ND) it scores 13.33 / 55.00 / 63.64 / 47.85. Without causal influence (CI) it scores 13.33 / 52.50 / 63.38 / 45.31. Without restart (RB) it scores 16.67 / 57.50 / 63.90 / 50.58. The fix has three parts: drop the 1/T normalization, add a Shapley-inspired causal-influence reward (similar steps grouped at cosine similarity >= 0.9, weight alpha=0.1), and add a verifiable <restart> reward (beta=0.1).
 quote: "Dropping either normalization or causal influence causes clear performance drops, showing their complementary role in discouraging shortcuts and promoting balanced contributions."
 where: Table 2, p.9; hyperparameters in B.2-B.3.
6. Training stability and a process-reward baseline. ReMA's training reward collapses (7B after about 150 steps, 3B after about 20). A process reward model (Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B) added per turn failed after about 30 steps, which the authors attribute to reward hacking.
 quote: "After 150 steps, ReMA collapses with its reward dropping to zero, whereas Dr. MAMR maintains stable training throughout."
 where: Sec 6.3 p.9; App G; H.2 (3B).
Minor: Inference-time restart prompting alone (ReMA+) gave about 8% gains on AMC23 and Olympiad at pass@1 and 7% on AIME24 and AIME25 at pass@16 (Sec 5.3, Fig 3). The Dr. MAMR vs ReMA gap on AIME25 widens as K goes from 1 to 64 (Fig 4c).

LIMITS
- Math reasoning only, Qwen2.5 Instruct 3B/7B/14B only. Both agents are the same weights with different role prompts, so this is not a heterogeneous or tool-using agent team. The reward is outcome-based with a verifiable answer.
- The headline gain over GRPO is small in places. On 14B, GRPO beats Dr. MAMR on MATH500 (80.60 vs 80.40) and GSM8K (94.50 vs 93.69). The paper does not report seeds or variance. Single runs on AIME24 (30 problems) move in steps of 3.33 points.
- "Lazy" is defined through attention-suppression KL, not human judgement. Laziness is a training-time artifact of the RL loss, so it does not show that inference-time multi-agent systems built from prompted agents behave this way.
- The causal-influence and restart rewards depend on an embedding-based step grouping, and alpha and beta were fixed at 0.1 "given the substantial computational cost". The restart behaviour needed an SFT cold start with GPT-4o-inserted noise (B.5).
- Internal inconsistency: Sec 6.2 says gains grow with larger base models, but H.1 says gains are "less pronounced on the 7B and 14B models" and attributes this to "weaker instruction-following". Table 3 shows the 3B gain over GRPO is +2.37 average, and the 7B gain is +3.35. Treat the scale claim cautiously.
- The ReMA vs ReMA+ comparison uses a prompt-only change at inference. The authors do not report a compute-matched comparison against single-agent sampling, apart from the pass@K plots.
- Pass@K plots (Fig 4c, Fig 8) are read from charts. The text gives no numbers.

BUILDS ON
- ReMA (Wan et al., 2025): the two-agent meta-thinking and reasoning framework.
- Multi-turn GRPO (Wan et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025), from GRPO (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025a, DeepSeek-R1) and DAPO (Yu et al., 2025).
- Dr.GRPO (Liu et al., 2025b), on token-level normalization; the authors say their analysis is distinct.
- Thought Anchors (Bogdan et al., 2025, arXiv): the attention-suppression influence measure.
- Shapley counterfactual credits for MARL (Li et al., 2021, KDD) and GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025).
- Classical lazy-agent MARL: Sunehag et al. 2018 (value decomposition), Foerster et al. 2018 (COMA), Castellini et al. 2022, Jaques et al. 2019.
- "LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation" (Laban et al., 2025): motivates restart.
- Training uses the Verl framework (Sheng et al., 2024) and DeepScaleR data (Luo et al., 2025).

CODE: none worth keeping. The reasoning agent's refined anti-laziness system prompt is in App C.1.2 (p.20), and the ReMA+ restart prompt is in App C.2.

FIGURES
- Fig 4(a), p.9, "Causal influence across training steps", ReMA vs Dr. MAMR (7B). It shows one agent's influence collapsing to zero under ReMA while both rise under Dr. MAMR. This is the single best picture of "one agent dominating".
- Alternative: Fig 1(a), p.4, a lazy vs non-lazy case study on the ELLIPSE question (full transcript in App D). The reasoning agent returns blanks and the meta-thinking agent computes 2520, whereas the non-lazy run gets 1260.

PROBLEMS: None embedded. Equations and figure axes are garbled in extraction, but the numbers I quoted come from clean text. I did not run the figures script.
